**Rate limits control admission; backpressure prevents accepted work from growing beyond service capacity.** For LLM requests, counting requests alone is often inadequate because prompt and generated-token lengths vary greatly. A short classification and a long document generation impose different loads. [1](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)[2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

Imagine a server that can process 10 requests per second while 12 arrive per second for a sustained period. Without rejection, scaling, or reduced work, the queue grows by roughly two requests per second. A bigger queue delays failure; it does not create processing capacity.

A token bucket admits bursts up to its capacity while refilling at a configured rate. Apply limits at suitable scopes, such as user, tenant, and shared service. Estimate or reserve token budgets for long generations, then reconcile with actual usage. Also limit concurrent requests, because memory pressure can become critical before a per-minute token budget is exhausted.

Use bounded queues and deadlines. When capacity is unavailable, reject promptly or tell callers when to retry rather than accepting work that will expire in the queue. Respect service-provided retry guidance. For transient failures, exponential backoff with jitter reduces synchronized retry storms, but retries must have a maximum count and overall time budget. [1](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

**Retries can worsen overload:** if each timed-out request produces several immediate attempts, arrival rate increases just when the service is struggling. Use a retry budget, shed low-priority work, and consider smaller outputs or cheaper models only under an explicit quality policy. Do not silently alter task semantics to improve throughput.

Measure queue wait, execution time, rejection rate, tokens per request, and tail latency separately. A healthy average can conceal a long tail of large requests. Fair scheduling and tenant isolation matter when one large customer can otherwise consume the shared queue. Validate the policy with bursty and long-output traffic rather than only uniform load.
